utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The situation as far as the availability of Judge Fluegge to hear the case has not changed. The Judges are still of the opinion that it's in the interests of justice to continue to hear the case; therefore, we sit 15 bis today as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to briefly address the following matter, that the Prosecution in yesterday's session raised the issue of 21 exhibits related to the current witness which are not currently part of the Defence's 65 ter list, with the Defence further indicating that it wished to formally ask for those exhibits to be added. The Chamber admitted one of those documents already - that's the D655 - although it has not yet dealt with the remaining documents, and the Defence is hereby instructed to make the necessary requests for the remaining documents at the time it intends to use them. Good morning, Mr. Sarenac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sarenac, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, to end any doubt, have you done with your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm done with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Mr. Sarenac --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to thank the witness for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sarenac, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You find Mr. Weber to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just in one follow-up matter from yesterday also on D655, Mr. Lukic and I did have the opportunity to communicate about its origin, and the Prosecution was informed that Mr. Lukic would inquire further with the Karadzic Defence, and that's how the matters stand right now. I just wanted to place that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll hear further from Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31361 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sarenac.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a 1st SMBR combat report dated 1 December 1993 from Veljko Stojanovic. Directing your attention to item 4, it states: "Milorad (son of Pavle) Golijanin born in 1932, 2nd pb was wounded around 0400 hours in Ozrenska Street by a rifle-launched grenade." Which is described also in the original as a Tromblona. According to this, he was wounded in the arm, leg and buttocks, and he later succumbed to his injuries in the Kasindol hospital. Is it correct that this individual who was injured belonged to the 2nd Battalion of your Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On the list that was shown to you yesterday, which is now D655, entry number 87 on page 5 of the document indicates that a Milorad Giljanin, son of Pavo, born in 1932, was injured in Ozrenska on 1 December 1993 as a result of a Tromblon. Is it correct that this is the same person who is mentioned in the report before you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I course, I mean, I cannot confirm or deny it now. I mean, because there are many people, many families with the last name of Golijanin and also first names, last names, father's names, et cetera. What is shown here is a report that should be trusted, the brigade commander -- now, it cannot be the same person there and here, of course. Because, as I've already said, there are so many Golijanins. There are so many people with the last name of Golijanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that it is the same person based on the similarity of name, similarity of father's name, date of birth, the manner of wounding, the date and the location of the wounding.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything more about all of that to you now. I can just say that the commander's report is truthful; the report of the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you know whether or not there were members of the Army of Republika Srpska on the list that you were shown yesterday when you were providing evidence to this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are lots of people on that list. I knew quite a few people who had been wounded, and what it says there is "wounded persons." I knew many people who had been wounded. I remember some of their last names and some of their first names, and I don't remember any specific first and last names except for the persons that I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you really haven't answered my question. Did you know whether or not there were members of the Army of Republika Srpska amongst those names on the list? If you knew, you knew; let us know. And if you didn't know, please let us know too.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know and I didn't recognise anyone there, any of the soldiers of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 31361 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31361 receives number P6777, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Witness, you said it cannot be the same person here and there -- I'm speaking at this moment. You said it cannot be the same person. Why can it not be the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. I saw this last sentence now or, rather, the last part of this sentence, "died at the Kasindol hospital." So this person was treated as a wounded person and then that person died. Now, how that person was treated there, I mean, well, that is different. How he was brought there, I mean, he was brought there as a wounded person and then he passed away there. But of course -- now, I cannot say. I cannot say that he was not on that list and that he mistakenly got on this list of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say I don't know, but it could be the same person. That's now your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31362 for the witness. The Prosecution -- if we could go please directly to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 24 September 1993 SRK regular combat report to the VRS Main Staff. Shortly we'll have item 7 of the report before us. There's reference to three soldiers being slightly wounded, including Mirko Trapara, who was born in 1927. Yesterday it seemed that you had some familiarity with certain members of the Trapara family. Did you know that Mirko Trapara was a member of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I talked about Bosko Trapara. He was well over 70 even at that time. I know that he was born exactly on the 7th of January, Orthodox Christmas, and that is why he was named Bosko. I knew him very well. I spoke about Bosko Trapara yesterday. However, there are many Traparas as well in the area of Lukavica, in the area of Kasindol, Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- you specifically, did you know that Mirko Trapara was a member of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I did not know specifically of Mirko Trapara personally. I mean, there were several thousand soldiers in my brigade so I couldn't, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answers the question. You apparently do not know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On that list you looked at yesterday, a few lines above one of the Traparas you commented on was a entry for Mirko Trapara born in 1927. Do I understand from your answers then that you did not consider whether this was a Mirko Trapara who was a member of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was born in 1927. There is no way he could have belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska at the time or, rather, he wasn't even subject to mobilisation. Now how he happened to be there and how they included him here, I really cannot say. It is probably because of his age that they classified him that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You really haven't answered my question again. Do I understand that you did not consider Mr. Trapara, whether he was a part of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps when you looked at that list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I think that the witness says that he could not be so therefore knowing what cannot be. At the same time, Witness, it comes as a bit of a surprise because the report that is shown to you talks about -- and that's a military report signed by Dragomir Milosevic as Chief of Staff talks about three soldiers, one of them being Mirko Trapara, born 1927. So to say it could not be that we have someone born in 1927 in the VRS, that needs a lot of explanation and why Mr. Milosevic is referring to this person born in 1927 as a soldier, if you say it can't be. So apart from whether you knew him or not, but your explanation, and perhaps you should stick rather to facts which are known to you rather than to start reasoning and arguing about what could and what could not be. You see this Trapara born 1927 referred to as a soldier in the report signed by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he maybe could have been a volunteer, but from my point of view, he couldn't have been mobilised. That's what I'm saying. Quite simply, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then apparently you are arguing. I mean, the basis for all these questions is a list about civilians being treated in Kasindol hospital. Mr. Weber seeks to establish that those on that list were not all civilians. Now, here, Mr. Trapara, and a person with a similar name appears, similar -- same year of birth appear on -- appears on that list, is called here a soldier, whether volunteer or whether he was in any other way arrived in the army, it's not very important, it's against being a civilian or not. And now you tell us it couldn't be because he's born in 1927. Please stick to the facts rather than to tell us what your opinion is. What could be, what could not be, stick to the facts. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 43 of your statement in this case, you state in part of the paragraph: "The document that has been shown to me," then there's a number relating to that list that we looked at, "seriously or gravely injured civilians hospitalised at the Kasindol hospital 1992, 1995, clearly shows a large number of civilians killed by enemy fire." And it continues, but I'll end the quote there. Had you ever seen this document before it was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That list, the list of injured persons, I saw it, of course. I didn't study it. I just recognised the people I knew myself, that I knew personally. I did not study the other information there, and I didn't have the opportunity of comparing whether any of them were soldiers or not, or in uniform or not, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I don't know how much time we are going to deal with this but, of course, at face value, it does to that extent -- I think the witness cannot be blamed for saying that. At the same time, you are exploring and you have explored the reliability of the information as being related to civilians or not. That's -- I mean, there's no need to make the witness admit that it may not be reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour. The Prosecution would tender 65 ter 31362 into evidence. And just for the record, the Prosecution maintains its position with respect to D655.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31362 receives number P6778, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6778 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just out of caution, I'd ask that the Chamber provide the witness a Rule 90(E) admonishment at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sarenac, I don't know what questions Mr. Weber will put to you, but he considers it appropriate to give you information about Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and I'll read that rule to you. And when it talks about a witness, you are the witness at this moment. "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness." Therefore, might tend to incriminate yourself. "The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way, shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." So if you think that a truthful answer to any of the questions Mr. Weber will put to you might tend to incriminate yourself, you may address me and then we'll decide whether or not you will be compelled to answer that question and what the consequences are. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Veljko Stojanovic was your brigade commander in the 1st SMBR?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Aside from a period between May and October 1995, is it correct that you were stationed in Lukavica throughout your time in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were one of the most senior officers at the Slavisa Vajner Cica or Cica barracks in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As part of your duties at the Cica barracks, you were responsible for monitoring the movement in and out of this compound; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I was responsible for discipline and everything else, this included.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "this included," it included movement in and out of the Cica barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Cica barracks was located to the north of the Slobodan Princip Selo barracks where the SRK command was located; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the relationship, as it were, between the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 19, you indicate that your units were provided with copies of extracts from international conventions describing the rules of conduct towards the enemy, prisoners, and civilian population and the provisions of international humanitarian law in general. Were you informed by your superiors about anything related to the use of prisoners for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, as far as our obligations are concerned, in terms of abiding by the rules of the Geneva Convention, it was not once but it was several times that we got photocopied or especially printed provisions of the Convention as to how prisoners from the opposing side should be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did they tell you that using prisoners of war for dangerous work details is contrary to the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they told us, and that was clear to me anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were then aware that placing prisoners in life-threatening conditions is prohibited.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarenac, at this time, I'm going to ask you to watch a video clip from a Sky News broadcast in September 1992 and then I will have a number of questions for you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play a portion of Exhibit P81. The time code for this would be 5 minute 25 seconds to 6 minute, 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About -- interpretation, is there -- for the record, does it have to be played twice or ...? It has to be played twice. You will look at it two times, that is because we prepare the interpretation during the first viewing, and then we'll receive the final interpretation or -- you, because I do not know whether it's -- the original is English or not, you will then receive or we will receive the final interpretation in the second viewing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I read the time codes from the original and we're just verifying the time codes on the clip, P81.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we'll now replay it from the, I believe, 1 minute 42 second line for the translation. Sorry, it's 1:48:49.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "At Kula, that does not happen, but the men are forced to work in fields close to Sarajevo's battle-grounds. Some are being hit out in the open, but more have suffered according to the prisoners when they are taken to dig trenches in Sarajevo's front lines in complete contradiction of all war conventions. "They take us in teams of ten to dig trenches between front line buildings, usually three dig and three others throw out up the earth. It's dangerous. One prisoner has been killed and two wounded. "The Serb warden promises the men will be released if an exchange can be arranged. But none of them are likely to ever be able to return to their home village, now firmly in Serb hands. Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I followed, for purposes of the interpretation, the B/C/S channel and I noticed that when Mr. Van Lynden, the reporter, was speaking, that it was not translated into B/C/S, if I observed that well. Could the B/C/S booth confirm whether the English spoken text was interpreted for the witness? And I move now to the B/C/S channel to hear the answer. Yes, I -- it's confirmed by the interpreters that it was read the first time and not in the second round and I listened in only in the second round, so this has been -- So you have received B/C/S translation for the whole of the clip. Then you may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarenac, were you aware of anything that is discussed in the video that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recognise this. I cannot relate it to myself or my job at the barracks or in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question was whether you were aware in whatever way, professionally, whether you heard it otherwise, whether you saw it, no limitations, were you aware of this or these kind of things happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard that people were used to do different sorts of jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "different sort of jobs," being baking and cleaning a room, or -- please tell us what you meant by "different sort of jobs."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] specifically at my barracks, shields were put up to protect from sniping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was not limited to your barracks, but at least you have told us that shields were put up. By prisoners? You are nodding, you are confirming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The labour platoon did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The labour platoon of prisoners? Did they have platoons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, they were not prisoners. They were both Serbs and Muslims, local residents who were not otherwise engaged in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that was not the question. The question is about what you saw here, and it is prisoners being used for dangerous jobs. Then it's of no use to tell us that those who were not prisoners did dangerous jobs because the issue is about prisoners doing dangerous jobs. By the way, I asked you what you meant by "different sort of jobs," what you heard, as you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not eye witness such things, nor did I issue orders for people to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our patience is limited, Mr. Sarenac. You were not asked whether you eye-witnessed anything. You told us you heard prisoners being used for different sort of jobs. The question is: What did you hear about these jobs to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably this included these jobs, they were probably used for digging. But I'm speaking in general. I don't know of any specific case. I did hear about such things. I was able to hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You heard this kind of jobs being included and that makes you believe that this probably has been the case. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed and try to answer in a more direct way to questions and not answer questions that are not put to you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to 65 ter 31279 for the witness. I'm just waiting, Your Honours, because I don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't have it on the screen either. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Before you is a copy of the statement from Zeljko Bambarez regarding an incident of 31 December 1993 regarding five working platoons from Grbavica and ten prisoners from Kula who were performing engineering works. At the bottom of the page, it states: "Accuracy of the copy verified by authorised official at the security organ." And then we see your name and a signature. Do you acknowledge that this signature is yours?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the third paragraph of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could go to the previous page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It indicates that people were working at the hilltop before Osmica and below Osmica. Is it correct that this area was in the immediate vicinity of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Toward the bottom of the page in both languages, Mr. Bambarez states that: "Dragan Lakanovic was there and I told him to watch the prisoners until I go to the hilltop and come back. I was there for maximum 10 minutes and I was returning. Lakanovic was shooting at four of them who had started to run away. Two more prisoners were at that spot, and I managed to take them out of the communication trench?" Is it correct that members of the 1st SMBR shot at prisoners who tried to escape?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a copy of that statement for certain purposes. Of course, I lost sight of it. I made a copy for some court or something. In any case, I had made a copy of that statement and I accepted that statement there as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, you are answering a question which is not put to you. The question was whether it's correct that members of this brigade shot at prisoners who tried to escape. If you know, tell us; if you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I remember, probably yes. I can only now -- I mean, I'm looking at this document now. I know that I had earlier made a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just look at the last page again. Mr. Sarenac, what do you mean by "having verified the accuracy of the copy"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement, accompanied by a certain document, was meant for the corps. It was written for the corps, and it was accompanied by some document. Now I don't remember what exactly it was. I didn't make it for any other purpose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you, Mr. Sarenac. That's not my question. My question is: What do you mean when you say you have verified the accuracy of this copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It confirms authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That what is contained in this document is authentic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you can only confirm authenticity after having read the entire document and satisfied yourself of the truthfulness of what is in the total document. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I verified the accuracy of the statement of Zeljko Bambarez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear my question? My question is: You can only determine authenticity after having read the document and satisfied yourself of the truthfulness of the content. And that's what you did. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you can answer the question then put to you by Mr. Weber that members of your brigade shot at prisoners who were escaping. That's accurate, according to your verification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the last paragraph of this document, which is at the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S and is on page 2 that is before us, Mr. Bambarez states: "I just want to mention that regardless of all dangers that were in places that were to be guarded (during the day a dozen bombs landed a metre or two away from me), I was with them all the time until that moment." I come back to this now because of your previous answers. Is it correct that you were aware that members of your brigade were taking prisoners to work in locations that were dangerous and were subjected to things like we see here, appears to be shelling. You were aware of this; right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you do anything to prevent the continued use of prisoners as part of dangerous work details?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position in the command of the brigade, in my specific organ, was not of that nature. I did not either plan the use of men or the building of fortifications, and I was not in a position to either decide that it would be done or to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't do anything, and we have your explanation now as to what you feel as why.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody asked me in advance whether it could be done or not. Everybody did their own job. I had so much work in my own area. I had no time to deal with this until this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31279 receives number P6779, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31319 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you is a statement from Drago Lakanovic who was referenced in the previous document regarding the same shooting incident that we just discussed. Could you please confirm that this is your signature at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution will also tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31319 receives number P6780, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31320 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you is a statement from Lieutenant Aleksandar Pandurevic, assistant commander for the intelligence and security, regarding the same incident that we are discussing. Again, is this your signature at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to these last two notes that we have seen, is it correct that you forwarded both of them to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. That's why they were done. Why else would they be?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 31320 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31320 receives number P6781, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31297 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a report written on your behalf, I see, to the penal and correctional facility Butmir Kula on designating prisoners for works in the Cica barracks. It appears that it's signed for you by Vojo Planincic. Could you please tell us who this person is.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Planincic was my deputy, my stand-in, and I was away at the time because my brother or cousin, Cedo, died, got killed on the 28th of May, 1993, and I attended the funeral in the village near Borik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On the bottom left side of the document, we see that it is handwritten "671-592 Soniboj. Take for processing immediately." Is it correct that that reference to Soniboj relates to an official at the Kula prison?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you -- we'll look at some more documents related to him in a little bit. But could you tell the Chamber right now what his position was.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time and later, he was the warden of that institution, Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the Kula prison during the war?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited on a couple of occasions. One of them was when the Muslims had shelled this facility some time in the spring of 1993, and that's when a relative of mine was killed, Sredoje Radojcic, who was in detention there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Kula prison is near the Lukavica barracks? And when I'm referring to that barracks, I'm referring to the command post of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, not your barracks, the Cica barracks.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was closer to the airport than to the barracks. It's about 2 to 3 kilometres from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31297 receives number P6782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31308 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you is a request signed and stamped by Lieutenant-Colonel Veljko Stojanovic dated the 1st of February, 1993 to engage 15 to 20 prisoners from the Kula prison for the consolidation of fortification features for combat operations and protection between 1 and 5 February 1993. Underneath this request it states: "The SRK intelligence and security organ agrees with the request of Lieutenant-Colonel Stojanovic regarding the engage of prisoners and recommends that the request be realised." As for the details on carrying it out, Captain Vojo Planincic has been designated from VP 5712. And then we see that this then contains the stamp and seal with the signature of Marko Lugonja, the chief of the intelligence and security organ of the SRK. This is the same Vojo Planincic who was your deputy; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were aware of these assignments that went through the brigade command and the SRK command?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in this case, I was, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 31308 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31308 receives number P6783, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to try and sneak in one quick document before the break, if I can. If the Prosecution could please have 65 ter 31305 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a request by -- another request by Lieutenant-Colonel Stojanovic dated the 24th of January, 1993 to engage 15 prisoners from the Kula prison to perform certain works, include the construction of installations and digging of trenches along the range behind the confrontation lines. The document that we just looked at before this appeared to be a request to have these prisoners continue this work. Is it correct -- were you aware of this previous engagement also which we see going through the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirmed the other one, but I was not necessarily even aware of this one. Not all the documents for the commander went through me. He never refers to myself or my organ here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31305 receives number P6784, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, admitted into evidence. Witness, may I take you -- before we take a break, may I take you back to one of your previous answers. When asked about whether you knew about these jobs and where you talked about that sort of "different sort of jobs," you said that you heard about prisoners being used for different sort of jobs. What kind of jobs these were, and you said "probably this included these jobs. They were probably used for digging. But I'm speaking in general. I don't know of any specific case. I did hear about such things. I was able to hear that." It's only a minute or two ago when you were asked: "Is it correct that you were aware of these assignments that went through the brigade command and the SRK command?" Your answer was: "Yes, in this case, I was, certainly." So, at one moment, you tell us that you have some kind of -- you heard something, some kind of general knowledge, no specific cases, you add there specifically. And five minutes later, when looking at the documents, you say, Yes, in this case, I was certainly aware of these assignments. Are you aware of perhaps -- or may I ask you, do you have any comment on why you say five minutes ago that you were not aware of any specific cases, and five minutes later, you say you were? If you have any comment. I just put it to you that that's what I observed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, after 20 years, these were not characteristic jobs. These were not things that went on all the time. After 20 years, I allow myself to say this. I'm almost 67 years old. And not having any documents that could have refreshed my memory, I mean, that's it. I had no other reason to deny that or to give any other kind of answer. I mean, no other reason. Because this was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you should have told us on from the beginning that if you had been unable to verify the documents, that your memory would not serve you sufficiently to answer those questions. What that would have meant for the Defence, whether to call you as a witness, yes or no, is a different matter, but whatever the reason may be, this Chamber does not expect you, on these points -- of course if it's a lack of memory, you say, I've forgotten it five minutes ago but now I know again, then that's your comment on what I just said. Leave it to that. You may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I'd like to put on the record that I failed to decide on document 31308, which was assigned number P6783. P6783 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I forgot to ask you something in relation to a previous document that we looked at. It was P6782. In that document, you were listed as the Barracks Commander Captain 1st Class Desimir Sarenac. Is it correct that you were the barracks commander for the Cica barracks?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, as the ranking officer in the barracks in the command, I had that position too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31295 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a report you authored dated 10 April 1994 that you sent to the SRK intelligence and security department with the subject line "Muslim prisoners escaping." In the first paragraph of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is the translation not available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no translation. Is it a document which originally stems from the Office of the Prosecution, or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is. And I do see that we do, I think, have a translation available for this document. We will work on it being uploaded. Your Honours, if I may proceed with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you slowly proceed and keep in mind that we may face some problems in the absence of an English translation, then for the time being, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph -- the first paragraph of this document where you list the names of four individuals, Mejfudin Hadzic, Midhat Hadzic, Ekrem Hadzic and then Savic Cosic, and then the area below these names where I believe it states: "The escape took place in the afternoon after the contractor, Vojislav Vukotic, took the prisoners to a military detention facility for accommodation at the end of a working day. Upon arrival to the detention facility one of the prisoners knocked on the detention facility warden's door while making a hand gesture to Vukotic as if the detention facility warden was in his office. Vukotic then left the prisoners at the detention facility." Do you see this information?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It then goes on to describe how the prisoners escaped in the course of the evening and the detention warden was not present at the time. Do you know the facility warden that's being referred to here in this document?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, it was Risto Bajago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the following paragraph, it indicates: "The said prisoner group in this composition had worked about one year on various jobs around the FSVC barracks under above-mentioned Vukotic's control. After their working day was over, they would be taken to their accommodation at the Kula KPD?" Do you see this information?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The reference to the barracks is a reference to the barracks that you were a command of; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In footnote 1, it indicates that Mr. Vukotic was a work contractor in the capacity of an army member. Could you please tell us what was Mr. Vukotic's role at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukotic was an elderly man born in 1925; you can see that here. He worked in maintenance when things were supposed to be repaired, like a facade that had been hit, or for instance, a wall, also taking care of the park within the barracks. That's what Vukotic did because he couldn't really do other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31295 receives number P6785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I put on the record that the English translation meanwhile appeared on our screens. And is it uploaded? It's already part of e-court so it has been uploaded in e-court as well. Therefore, nothing prevents us from admitting it. It's admitted into evidence. I have one additional question, Witness. We see that prisoners were used for certain jobs and that they were imprisoned, for example, in the Butmir prison or -- well, they are borrowed from penitentiary institutions or detention facilities. Do you know - if you don't know tell us - whether these were prisoners of war or were they civilians detained awaiting exchange or whatever? Could you tell us what their status was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in this case, it would be very hard for me to determine their status. Because, for already a year, the same people had been working there. Probably they were prisoners of war. I think that would be it. Maybe they were waiting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why do you think that? We've seen earlier that military officials ask for prisoners to be sent to them where nothing indicates that these are prisoners of war, and the Chamber has received evidence that persons were detained, being civilians waiting for exchange. What makes you believe that these persons who --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I put here in the heading, Muslims of -- prisoners of Muslim ethnicity escaping. So they were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. But why, that was my question, why did you quickly say "must be prisoners of war" rather than civilians being detained? What makes you so quickly jump to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know even now. I hadn't even seen all of this, but this is what the document specifically says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What does the document say about them being prisoners of war or civilians being detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the English booth, please. Interpreter's note: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear you now, but we missed the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said that's what the heading says, prisoners of Muslim ethnicity escaping. That's what the heading says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, apparently then that's on your mind that if you were a Muslim prisoner, that you must be a prisoner of war rather than a civilian being imprisoned for good or bad reasons. This Chamber received evidence that civilians were detained as well, and that's the reason why, in the beginning, I asked you whether you know, and I gave you an opportunity to say that you don't know. And apparently, from what I see now, you're trying to draw conclusions from what you see as a text on the screen, whereas the only thing I'm interested in is whether you know something, not what your conclusions are on the basis of what you see on the screen, as you say, not being familiar with those documents. So you don't know. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the status of these persons was specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a slightly different question to ask. You told us that you were the warden of these barracks where these prisoners came from; is that not -- is that correct? If you can answer in words rather than by nodding so that the record can reflect your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was trying to indicate that I was following what you were saying. As for this, in my barracks, prisoners were not held. It's only people who had fled from the other side, but they just stayed there for a while and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Just answer my question, please. The barracks from which these prisoners were taken for a year to go and work, was it the barracks of which you were a warden?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, just to interrupt you, I believe he said he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Commander. Commander of, yes, you were the commander of that barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And for a year you authorised these workers to go out and do work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They worked within the compound of the barracks, and they were taken to the KPD Kula and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not my question. Did you authorise the release of these prisoners for a year to go out to work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They worked with Vojo Vukotic, an old man born in 1925, and they did not have any other security. They were trusted to such a degree. I mean, there was no other security there. They were just together. And they repaired certain things within the barracks. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's not answering my question. You authorised their use to do the work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go on to 65 ter 31298, sub-letter A, for the witness. And the Prosecution would note that the full version of this material is available under 31298 but for the use in court today, we've tried to streamline the amount of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, just so you have an explanation, this is a notebook, it's specifically coming up before you, it will be excerpts from the notebook containing information on the daily activities of the Kula prison from 3 January 1993 through 3 November 1993. This notebook was recovered by the Office of the Prosecutor on 9 July 2003 at the Kula detention centre, formerly known as KP Dom Butmir Ilidza. I just wanted you to have that context before we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 4 of the B/C/S and page 5 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is an entry of 24 January 1993. On this page, we see a chart containing a list of various work sites, which includes the SVC barracks under item 7. Are you familiar with these work sites that are listed here?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to be going through many entries, so I will come back and ask you about the specific ones as we go through the entries. On the right-hand side column, below the column "remarks," we see Dobrinja and below it, there is a list of names. At the bottom of the page under this column, it states: Hadzic, Mejfudin, and Borcilo, Nihad on the approval of warden S. Soniboj." And underneath that, we see that there's an arrow next to which it states: "With the approval of Warden Skiljevic." Is this the same Warden Soniboj of the Kula facility that you referred to earlier today?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably. I didn't know another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, who, then, is also then Warden Skiljevic?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the warden, Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The warden of where?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The warden -- well, of that institution, Kula. I mean, that institution, that prison. He was the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the document that we just looked at before coming to this notebook, we saw the name Mejfudin Hadzic appearing in a report to the SRK security intelligence organ. And this was the same document that referred to this individual being taken out for work details for almost a year. Is it correct that this is the same Mejfudin Hadzic that was mentioned in your report from April 1994?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that for sure because this is a different location, Dobrinja. Who was working there, I don't know. I cannot claim that it's one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Nor could you exclude it; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot exclude it either, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, just so you know, on that previous page 1, the work sites that was listed on it that you said that you were familiar with was Dobrinja, so I am going to ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you do so, Mr. Weber, I noticed that at the bottom of this page, it says that this is page 1 out of 8, whereas the cover page is 1 out of 21, and the third page is 1 out of -- is number 2 out of 21, and the fourth page is -- there is something odd in the numbering of the pages which is also reflected if you look at not the official e-court pages but the way in which we find them listed. We see that it jumps from 1 and 2, then to 4, 5, 6, 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, a very simple explanation for that is that there were multiple different translations that were requested for parts of this at different times. For the sake of coherence, the Prosecution has ordered these translations, the segments from them, in chronological order as they actually appear in the original which we've also excerpted. So I appreciate that the numbers may be different at the different pages because they relate to different partial translations. They appear in the sequential order which they do in the original document in this upload.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we have to look in the original to see whether this is really chronologically in order. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is an entry from 3 January 1993. It states that a prisoner named Izudin Hodzic was wounded in the left thigh by a sniper round in Dobrinja at 1245 hours. Is it correct that you are aware that this area is close to the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you aware of prisoners being hit by sniper fire while they were doing work near the confrontation lines in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, I see this case but I do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not isolating it to a particular case. I'm asking you more generally. Were you aware that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I cannot remember a particular example.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go through some more examples. There's an indication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, no one asked you for an example. They asked whether you had general knowledge of this thing happening. And even without knowing that on one day this happened, you can tell us whether or not you were aware of these kind of things, even if you don't know the details, were happening. I have to stress again that you have to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I allow for the possibility that I knew of that, but now I'm saying specifically that I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer to the question. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We see here that Mr. Hodzic received medical assistance. Do you know if prisoners were taken to the Kasindol hospital to receive medical assistance from injuries that they received at the front lines either as a result of sniping or shelling?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Going on to another entry. Could the Prosecution please have page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, are you able to tell us where this specific witness might have received treatment? Did I say "witness"? Oh. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I suppose it could have been provided at Kula, but I cannot be sure. I know that there was no other medical institution to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 5 of the B/C/S and page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, on this page we will see an entry for 2 February 1993, and we see a similar chart as we looked at before listing various work sites. At the bottom of the page, and if we could go to page 8 in the English, it states: "The Muslim prisoner Izudin Hodzic was killed by the Muslim side, by sniper, at the Zlatiste work site." Sir, this work site is also by the confrontation lines; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, earlier in this same notebook, we saw that this individual Izudin Hodzic was shot by sniper fire in Dobrinja. Is it your evidence that you were not aware of the continual use of prisoners at the front lines? Here we have an example where an individual appears to have been taken out on two different occasions to two different locations, shot and injured the first time, and then killed a month later. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, I don't know what the circumstances were, where they went, where they worked. I was probably notified and this is the warden's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, could we look at the previous page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, at the bottom of that page, it's written: "Five men were taken to Kasindol hospital for a checkup at 11.40 with Milan Vasic and were returned at 12.40." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does this mean that some of these men that were prisoners and had been injured here are taken to the Kasindol hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to be so, looking at this. But the prison was not in my purview. I cannot provide any further comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the prison. I'm just wanting to establish that prisoners were sent to Kasindol hospital for medical attention. Remember we spoke about a list of civilians yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's obvious, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 6 of the B/C/S and page 9 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is an entry that relates to 6 February 1993. A prisoner named Nihad Mehmedovic was wounded in the arm by shrapnel at the Krtelji work site. Could you please tell us where this work site was located? It's one of the ones that you said you were familiar with on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the place name. Krtelji is close to the airfield, it's about 4 kilometres from my barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We see here that Mr. -- that this individual was transferred to the Kasindol hospital. Just following up on Judge Moloto's question, is this again another incidence where we see that someone who is injured by shrapnel was taken to the Kasindol hospital?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now supposed to interpret somebody else's document, but it seems evident from what is written, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were providing comments on the Kasindol hospital yesterday at transcript page 26105, you stated: "The hospital treated both uniformed personnel and civilians." Could you explain to us why you did not tell the Chamber that the hospital also treated prisoners who were injured during work details?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Although it never crossed my mind, and I did not deal with these matters. But the only medical institution that was specialised in providing all assistance was that one. Military uniformed personnel was only temporarily accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, just so you're aware, our case would not be that you're totally unaware of these events. It would be that you are the commander of the Cica barracks and, as we've seen, you've authored documents related to the use of these prisoners. Do you have any comment on that observation?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. What are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm putting to you is the fact that you are claiming to be unaware of certain -- unaware of matters relating to the use of prisoners at the front lines. That's not totally accurate. That as commander of the Cica barracks and an individual who authored a number of documents related to these prisoners as part of work details, that you are, in fact, aware of the use of prisoners on the front lines and them being injured.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't deny that especially when you refreshed my memory. I confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through some more entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 12 of the B/C/S and page 17 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is an entry related to 28 February 1993 and a Muslim prisoner named Isme Hidic who was killed by a sniper round at the Novakovici work site. Could you please tell us where this work site was.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novakovici is a village on the periphery of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This entry indicates that Mr. Hidic was transferred to the Lukavica hospital, to the morgue. Was there a Lukavica hospital? Is this a different hospital than the Kasindol hospital or is it the same?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably Kasindol hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 11 of the B/C/S and page 15 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the bottom of this page it states: "On 27th February 1993, at 1700 hours, two persons of Muslim nationality, Mehmed Simic and Safet Hrapo, were detained from Vogosca and escorted by Sasa Blagovcanin, member of the Vogosca Brigade Military Police." Then there's a note: "The detained persons have visible injuries." Below this in the original - and if we could have the next page of the English translation - it states: "The persons who worked at the work place near Sucuri complain that they dare not go to the above-mentioned work place because they have been maltreated and physically beaten." Were you aware of these prisoners being physically beaten? Is it correct this happened?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases that I was aware of, I took steps, I heard of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How many such cases did you hear of, of prisoners being physically beaten?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I remember two cases when I took disciplinary measures. I suggested that the commander of the military police be replaced for allowing force to be used against the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My question wasn't exactly limited to instances where you did something. How many cases did you hear of prisoners being physically beaten?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anymore how many cases I'd heard of. But this was not constant practice, and my policemen and everybody who worked with the prisoners knew very well that I don't tolerate such things. I don't allow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 9 of the B/C/S and page 12 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask first. Did you make a record of the disciplinary measures that you took against those who did do these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I reported to the commander and made a record. And when it was not within my jurisdiction to take measures, I suggested measures to the commander. But our records are now scattered all over the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you do when taking measures was within your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned the replacement of the military police commander, that something the commander did at my proposal, and I proposed disciplinary measures to the commander suggesting that such persons be removed from their units because such people should not be allowed to work with prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you take any disciplinary measures yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Disciplinary measures, such as remand in custody, et cetera, were not within my purview, within my powers. I could propose them to the commander. I could also propose that the person be transferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your position, you had no disciplinary powers at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for this type of infraction. It was a more serious violation to be dealt with by the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any written -- did you write to the commander that you would seek disciplinary measures to be taken against -- apart from this one example, you say, but this -- what I see is, I would say, a constant system of the use of prisoners for labour and now also ill-treatment and beatings of prisoners. Did you ever take any measures? Did you write any reports about this or suggested disciplinary matters to be taken, rather than the prisoners to be taken out again the day after that or beatings to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were relatively few cases when prisoners were used in the zone of our barracks to build fortifications. They worked mostly on the maintenance of the barracks and its structures. Now, talking about KPD Kula, if you ask me to comment, I understand that you may have the impression that I was aware of all this. But I couldn't be aware of all this and I couldn't propose any measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And about the beatings, what did you do? If someone would beat a prisoner, you'd have no way of disciplinarily responding to such a situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brigade commander would do that after receiving my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you write any reports, and this repeats my previous question, about your people beating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote reports to the commander about that. I reported to him either orally at briefings or in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Lukic, it might be important to retrieve such documents which would support the testimony of the witness. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, Judge Moloto, did you have a question? I didn't mean to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just pondering but -- the witness is changing from what he said a few minutes ago when I asked him questions, he said to me he did discipline people and I then asked him whether he had records of that. And I also wanted to find out if those records could be found. Then he said they were all scattered all over. Now, in response to Judge Orie, he now says he didn't discipline. He only reported to his commander. I find this to be inconsistent with what he told -- how he answered my question. Do you have any explanation for this inconsistency, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I said that disciplinary measures were meted out, not that I did so myself. I knew from the start that I was not able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You think so, but I'm telling you, you didn't say so. You told me you took disciplinary measures. And I asked you, did you keep a record of the disciplinary measures that you took, and you said to me they were scattered all over the show.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the disciplinary measure that I took was proposing them to the commander or the competent person who would do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to page 9 in the B/C/S and page 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, on this page, we see two entries from 13 February 1993. The first entry relates to a woman named Fatima Bajramovic who tried to escape by jumping through an upper-floor window, and she was apprehended near gate 1 and placed in solitary confinement. The second entry relates to a Mirela Granulov who was taken over by Mr. Vasilje Vidovic pursuant by a request of the SRK command. My first question: Were you aware that females were being kept in detention at the Kula facility?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must ask for your understanding. You are showing me documents or, rather, the notebook kept by the warden of Kula asking me to comment. I did not know what was going on at Kula prison. How could I know? I knew only some details that were pertinent to us. How could I possibly comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in your evidence, in your evidence in this case, you've commented on things that happened great distances away from your barracks, all the way over on the other side of the confrontation line, more than 5 kilometres away from where you were at. The reason I am asking you this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness, in his statement, is dealing what was his job. That was his task towards the end of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's far away from -- that was his job. In relation to this document, witness mentioned several times that he did not have anything with Kula prison, that he did not anything especially [sic] with their log-books. So the distance where something happened is not the issue but what was his task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is granted. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To be -- you could be surprised that -- without giving you an opportunity to respond to that, but I can tell you that when I consulted with Judge Moloto a minute ago before Mr. Lukic raised his objection, I -- we discussed exactly the same matter, as a matter of fact, and where I would have intervened otherwise spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why, unlike normal for objections, I didn't give you an opportunity to respond. But if you want to rephrase the question. The bottom line is the following: The witness in his position could expected to have knowledge about matters that were related to Kula to the extent that they borrowed prisoners from there, et cetera, et cetera. Now, for a general knowledge on other matters about what happened in the Kula prison, you would have to lay a foundation to start with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, I'm asking you about these matters because they -- is it correct that they -- all these work sites relate to areas in the zone of responsibility in which you were commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we continue -- Mr. Mladic, you will not speak aloud. Let that be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe my colleague Weber should mention which areas, Since he just mentioned Vogosca. And I think that could be -- create a misunderstanding since Vogosca is not in the area of responsibility of this gentleman. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With the exception of the Vogosca, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's better to enumerate the sites than go with exceptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you could do is, Mr. Weber, you could have a look at the list at the workplace and, for example, the kitchen, I do not know whether the kitchen was within or not. I saw that as one of the places. So, therefore, it's -- you have to ask yourself what kitchen, where? Apparently, you're apparently linking this to the examples which we find here on this page. That link still has to be established as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I didn't mean to necessarily do that, Your Honours. I see we're at a break also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're at a break time. And this allows you to further consider, Mr. Weber, where the boundaries are of what we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, if I could tender the document and then I can move on to some other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object to tendering this document through this witness since obviously he has no knowledge about the document, nor it is in connection with his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's in connection to his testimony, Mr. Lukic, and that's the test. Not whether you included it in the statement, yes or no, but he has been questioned about it in quite some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree. But he has no knowledge about this log-book really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with that. At the same time, for admission of evidence, which is directly related to the subject matter of the testimony of the witness, it's the -- this Chamber has often admitted into evidence documents, whether you call it from the bar table or not, but in a direct relation to the testimony of the witness. Therefore, the objection is denied. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31298A receives number P6786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. We take a break. Mr. Sarenac, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to assist while the witness is coming in. Actually, the Prosecution is going to go to one more entry in P6786. If we could go to page 22 of the B/C/S and page 29 of the English. And, Your Honours, I do acknowledge receipt of the urgent motion that the Defence filed today relating to the addition of the documents to the Defence 65 ter list. I can respond to it at the end of the examination, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd do so, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can I have the next page in the B/C/S. I have it as page 22. Which I actually believe is page 23 in the B/C/S is what I'm looking for. Can I see the previous page in the B/C/S. Maybe it's page 22. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
