utterances.text: Mr. Sarenac, I wanted to go through one more entry with you in the notebooks. I'm just waiting for it to come back. At the bottom of the page in the original version, it indicates that you brought a woman to the Kula prison on the 15th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I believe if we can turn to the next page in the B/C/S and we don't have the corresponding English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that what we just went away from the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It was page 29 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And it also indicates that you, Captain 1st Class Desimir Sarenac, brought this woman to the KPD Kula and at that same time you brought another woman. Sir, I'm going to pose to you again: Is it correct that you were aware that women were being kept at the Kula prison?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot see that clearly, this content. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, it was in the previous page in the B/C/S so if you need time to look at it, let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could see the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you see it towards the bottom of the page, starting with "Dana 15 X 93," the second one.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you need to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could have the next page for the witness, just to make sure he sees the whole entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, it continues on to the top. Do you see that you also brought a second woman to the Kula KPD at the same time that you brought the first woman.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that they were brought there. And I see down here that a visit is being mentioned. I don't know in what status they were brought there, to visit someone or something like that. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I read to you what it reads there and then please, think about your answer and about the question before you continue. What you are referring to, and apparently you are trying to get a quick impression to order to see whether that is relevant: "The warden has approved a visit for prisoner of war, Goran Bojic. The visit was from his mother, Hasmeta Bojic." So the women mentioned here have got nothing to do -- as the document is taken at face value -- has got nothing to do with the women you were asked about. Please focus on the question whether you were aware that women were detained. And if it helps you, I can tell you that about Amna Kovac, the document reads that she was taken into custody. So stay away from your own possible explanations and your suggestions that one of the persons may have been a visitor where the document tells us that she was in custody and that the visitor was a totally different person. Now, would you please answer the question that was put to you by Mr. Weber. And our patience is not unlimited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this Amna Kovac, I remember that, for a while, she was staying at my barracks or guarded in my barracks. A person with that name and surname was brought there to be in my barracks until her exchange. So I made sure that she was kept there so that this Serb woman, Jovanka, would take care of her so that nothing unpleasant would happen to her. Amra, or Amna, whatever her name is, Kovac was brought from Foca and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you are not answering the question. The question is simple: Are you aware that women were being kept in the Kula detention unit? Your answer is very simple. Either you say yes, or you say no, or you say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whether they were. But as for this Amna Kovac, I think I took her there for that exchange, and probably this other woman was there with her. So from my barracks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not being asked what for did you take her there. The question is: You are aware that she was there. You took her there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think specifically, as far as Ms. Kovac is concerned, I took her there for an exchange because they brought her and she was supposed to stay there where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were not being asked for what purpose. You were being asked whether you took her there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I took her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you want to explain that in detail. Was she exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She was probably exchanged because she did not return after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking for conclusions. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where my function stops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, you may not know. That's fine. Then you tell us that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know, yes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What was the reason why she was taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For some reason, she had been in Foca until then. They brought her there for this exchange, so that she would wait for this exchange. Why she wasn't in Kula -- at any rate, they brought her to the barracks for some reason, and I made sure that she had accommodation there and Jovanka was staying with her. I remember that name. That was a young girl and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was she free to leave, to move out and not to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't dare allow that. This was a cautionary measure. While she was there, I can't remember how many days, it wasn't a question of months, it was less than that. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the length. I'm talking about why she was in detention. Whether she was free to leave, if she wanted to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm saying now I did not detain her. She was brought to me waiting for an exchange. And then when they told me from Kula that I should take her out, that happened. And I had the obligation to protect her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You detained her, or at least you were in charge of guarding her for the time she was with you when you brought her to Kula, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To take care of her, of course. I didn't have any other obligations or authority, as far as she was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If she would have asked you, Could I just go where I want to go and leave you, would that have been permitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was responsible for her and I had to hand her over, just as she had been brought to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So she couldn't -- she couldn't move freely out. You would keep an eye on her so that she would stay with you until you had delivered her in Kula.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not within my authority. This was done by exchange commissions and so on, since it was not safe for her to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not safe for her, you say, to move around freely. It wasn't safe for anyone at that time to move around freely, isn't it? I just want to put it clearly to you that this document clearly suggests that she is not free to move, that she is accompanied by you, that you deliver her at Kula prison where she's taken into custody which, in every day language, is called "detention." Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She was not with me. She was in my facility. She was guarded by the police. I mean, I made sure that she was guarded, taken care of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So where it reads "Captain 1st Class, Desimir Sarenac, brought her ..." that is untrue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's true, certainly, because when they asked me to bring her there, then I did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then she was with you. If I bring a person somewhere, and if that person is not free to move, that person is with me, and upon arrival in Kula prison, apparently she was taken into custody. Let's -- Mr. Sarenac, it doesn't make -- if you say the document is not forged, it's not a fraudulent document, let's face it, let's face what the document says. And I invite you to do that in relation to all documents that are put to you to the extent you are able to do so. If you do not know something, tell us. If you do know, tell us. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was just going to go through this last entry. I was going to move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, we're leaving this notebook right now, and I want to ask you about a different event. Is it correct that approximately 300 non-Serb detainees were bused to the Cica barracks from Hadzici on 22 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were ordered to prepare space for them and secure them?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who did you receive this order from?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this order from the commander to prepare premises for putting up so many people. They brought them by bus, and I ensured their safety and security so that they could be put into the facility where the military was. They were put upstairs and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the answer is, "I received this order from the commander." Because the question was: Who did you receive this order from? I know that you apparently feel a need to then give us a picture about how well you cared for all these people and how responsible you were, because that's the answer to every question, how well you were of all those people which you said you looked after and where others say were detained. Please stick to the question. You received the order from the commander. What's the next question, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this the commander of the brigade or the commander of the corps?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably commander of the brigade. It certainly wasn't the corps commander. I know that I got the order from the commander. Most probably it was the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was his name? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't have that picture before me now. Veljko Stojanovic was my brigade commander from the start; it probably was him. I cannot say it was him or maybe his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that these prisoners were kept in the dormitory at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31359 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you is a BiH MUP SDB statement from a male who is a graduated jurist from Hadzici. In this statement, this person describes what happened during his time at the Cica barracks in June 1992. I'd like you to focus on a part in the middle part of the document where this individual states: "On 22 June 1992, we, together with other 280 detainees, were taken in the buses of TRZ Hadzici to Lukavica to the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks." Then there's four names of individuals who drove the buses. It then continues: "After being physically abused for almost three full days in the night of 24 to 25 June 1992, all prisoners, that means about 280 of us, were shoved into a dormitory and then a person unknown to me called the names of a number of prisoners (we later determined 48 men were called over) and they were taken somewhere." We see this individual then goes on to explain that the remaining prisoners were taken to Kula and he did not learn anything about what happened to the 48 men who were taken away. Is it correct that this is what happened to those individuals who came from Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. I did not have any authority over this group of people. They came and I think that, as a matter of fact, immediately on the following day - because we did not have the opportunity to provide security for them there limitlessly because it was right at the front line - they were taken away on buses, just as they had been brought in. As for this, no way. No way. That I know for sure. No way. That somebody from the barracks, Slavisa Vajner Cica, was singled out of this group and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that you're not providing truthful evidence, that you're not providing truthful evidence about your responsibility as the commander of this barracks and these events that are depicted before us. Do you have any other comments?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had this happened, I would have known about it, unless it happened in some magical way without me knowing about it. I just know of this: When my people put them up there, they searched them on their own, and they brought a few tuna cans and I made them return all of that to these people. That was the only incident. As for all of this, no way. I would have known. I'm not an irresponsible person to claim something like this. These are masses of people. I would have known about it. How could this have been done without me knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. I've put my case to you so I'm going to move on. Is it correct -- to a different topic now. Is it correct that people who were leaving the city of Sarajevo told you that they had no food or electricity and the living conditions inside the confrontation lines were difficult? If you could just please provide me with a yes or no and then we'll look at some documents.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is because it's a compound question. Mr. Weber, you can expect this. Mr. Weber will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did people who were living in the city of Sarajevo tell you that they faced poor living conditions inside the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those who were brought to us, yes, there were such things that were stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31299 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to do with 31359?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- the Prosecution has led other evidence about this event, and I'd specifically refer the Chamber to P2225. And, on that basis, since there's already information before the Chamber in relation to this event, I was not going to seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is an explanation report you drafted on 16 December 1992 related to an interview with someone you classified as a defector from the Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page, it appears that you document the attempts of this individual and others who were attempting to cross the runway and were turned away by UNPROFOR. On this page, the report also states the following: "On this attempt to cross the runway, two families were with him who had two and three children respectively; for one of the families this was their 13th attempt to cross the runway." The next sentence states: "Apart from the wish to rejoin his family, Ferid also explains his exit with difficult living conditions in the city -- no food, electricity, cold and so forth and that due to this, UNPROFOR is catching from between 100 and up to 400 people every night at the airport attempting to make it across whose sole objective is to leave Sarajevo." Is it correct that this is the type of information you received?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it must be that way, otherwise why would it be written.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender 65 ter 31299 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31299 receives number P6787, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution actually go to 65 ter 31292, page 57. It's the witness's previous Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to change topics again and discuss the morale of the forces opposing the SRK. First I'm going to read to you what your recorded testimony in the Karadzic case was. During this testimony, you were asked: "And whatever potential they might have had, Lieutenant-Colonel, you knew, didn't you, that the morale amongst the 1st Corps forces was low and continued to diminish as the war went on, their forces were dying in large numbers, they had problems with -- and they had problems with mass desertions; isn't that correct?" You answered: "Yes, such information was available, of course." Do you stand by this testimony?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was of variable nature. Sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the living conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution now please go to 65 ter 31300.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 23 July 1993 1st SMBR security organ report from you based upon information you received from a defector. In the second paragraph, you state: "Information on the state of the enemy army's morale across the territory of Sarajevo where they have been stricken with panic following the latest successes of the Serb army, in particular, the fear and refusal to go out to Mt. Igman, which confirms our earlier information of people avoiding going out of Sarajevo at all cost." Do you see this information?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What were the "latest successes of the Serb army" which you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the linking up of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps with the Herzegovina Corps to break this corridor towards Herzegovina, towards the south and southeastern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I thought that might be what you're referring to. Is it correct that's Operation Lukavac 93?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31300 receives number P6788, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31273 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is another 1st SMBR security organ report also drafted by you dated a few days earlier, 18 August -- or, actually, excuse me, dated actually later, 18 August 1993, based on information received from another defector. Looking at the third-to-last paragraph on the page, I believe in both versions, we see a reference to figures around 400 Muslim soldiers killed. And then moving to the next paragraph, it reads: "It is widely known about the weapons and shortage of ammunitions. It is important to mention that a considerable number of weapons were lost when fleeing from Golo Brdo." Do you see the references that I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you possessed information about a shortage of weapons and of ammunition of the ABiH, that they faced these shortages?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the statement of this Goran Jovicic who defected, and I provided that report, although we couldn't be 100 per cent sure that it was correct. It was only his opinion. That's why it was forwarded to the analytics department in the corps command. That's how he could see, that's how he saw the situation at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, most of the documents that you comment on as part of your statement are similar to this. They're statements by individuals of things they told you when they came over the front lines. Would your comment that you just made about those statements being possibly not 100 per cent sure and they were forwarded to the corps command, would that also apply to those other materials? This wasn't checked information, I guess, to cut it short; right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the information had been checked; other aspects were not. They were collated in a certain place in order for conclusions to be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31273 receives number P6789, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let's try to go through one more document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question to you. You said, Well, this is the opinion of Goran Jovicic, therefore, whether true or not. Now, especially on the issue raised by Mr. Weber, that is the weapons and shortage of ammunition, there you do not say Jovicic tells us, but you say it is widely known. Therefore, if you say, Well, I just passed on this opinion of Mr. Jovicic, at least the language in this paragraph suggests otherwise: That it is widely known. Do you have any comment on this observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We used to receive such reports. And, generally speaking, it was known that they had a deficit, a shortage of ammunition and weapons, relative to the number of men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, your earlier explanation when asked about it whether this -- that you said, Well, it's just the information of one person, it's -- it goes beyond that. That's at least how I understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly we had more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31302.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 1st SMBR Official Note dated 10 August 1993. It also indicates it's drafted by you. If we could look at the first sentence of the note, we see that it is based on information received from a Ms. Natasa Miskin. In the next paragraph, we see that she was employed in Juka's unit doing tasks such as serving meals, cleaning and nursing. Is it correct that the reference to Juka's unit is Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Natasa Miskin, a young girl who left together with the UNPROFOR and provided that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please focus on my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please listen to the question and answer that question. Of course she provided the information at least that's reported. The question was whether Juka's unit was Juka Prazina's unit. Is that how you understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we look further down on the page at the last full paragraph of e-court page 1 in the English translation, and actually I think it is the first paragraph on e-court page 2 of the B/C/S. I might be off on this. We read the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks as if the -- it's the end of page -- the layout perhaps is slightly different but it seems that the text is corresponding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We read the following: "This brigade does not go into action; not all of them have rifles -- they only have between 30 and 35 rifles and there are 200 to 250 soldiers, including logistics." Is it correct that this is the information you had about Juka Prazina's unit?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received this information and we accepted it with a grain of salt until further verification. It was the way you see it written here pending further checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31302 receives number P6790, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could ask just one more question based on what the witness just said. If we can have page 2 in both versions of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of this page, the final paragraph says: "The information provided by Natasa Miskin can be considered on the whole to be reliable and are important for the identification of persons in units, therefore, in this sense the material is interesting for a follow-up." This was your assessment of this information that was provided to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I provided that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I see it's break time, Your Honour. I'm off on that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber. Is there any chance that you would finish before the break because then you would have approximately the two hours, which is more than the initially indicated one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm a little bit behind in time, but I can try to -- I will be slightly over time, Your Honours. I'll try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are requesting whether you are allowed to go over time? I have no answer to that question yet, Mr. Weber. Don't expect automatically --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I don't. And I'm going to try to accommodate the exact time provided by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you are at one hour, 43 or 44 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If that's the case, I would be approximately two hours, which was my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I asked you whether there was any chance that you could finish by the break which would be 12 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you're missing three or four minutes, I'm aware of that. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to come right close to my actual estimate of two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to a couple of questions related to documents in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 1D03039.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is another one of the Official Notes that you drafted. This one -- actually, I see it's signed by a Djordje Kovac, and it's associated to your statement. According to your statement, paragraph 14, this document shows that the members of the 1st Motorised Mountain Brigade of the ABiH were also deployed to positions outside the city of Sarajevo. But if we look at the first sentence in the third full paragraph on page 3 in the English, it states: "The 1st Motorised Brigade has been decimated." Reading on in the same paragraph, it says: "Certain companies go to Igman every 15 days but because of the shortage of men they rotate shifts every 3/3 days although the usual is to rotate them every 3 to 6." Why did you not include any comments on this information as part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which passage? I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is the Prosecution now dictating us what should we include in the statements of our witnesses? We included a document. We never dictated the Prosecution what they should have in their statements. And it's not the witness who composed the statement. I'm telling that from the beginning of this case. It is the members of the Defence. If there is anybody to be blamed, it's us. Not the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it very much depends on the circumstances. If, as you say, the Prosecution would blame you, then they would have first to establish that you had received or not sought the information the Prosecution considers appropriate to be included in a statement. Now, very often, you're perfectly right that if you put a statement or a document to a witness and you ask certain questions about it, then you would not, under all circumstances, expect a witness to go through that document and then to raise all kind of other things. To that extent, you're perfectly right. Sometimes it also happens that something that almost bangs into your eyes if you read the document are ignored both by the ones who are questioning and the ones who are responding to the questions. So it very much depends on the circumstances. I have at this moment, I invite --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may add something else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We wanted to include 130 documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- with this witness. We knew it was not possible. We cut it to 22, 23. And, of course, that we didn't cover everything he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but this was a document that was put to him, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was the document that was put to him and what we were interested with this witness, and it was obvious from his statement is the kind of work he did observing the enemy positions, and which positions did the enemy at that time in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I was just about to ask Mr. Weber --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we do not know Mr. Weber or cross [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Lukic, you're now interrupting me, which I am not entirely happy with. Mr. Weber, please think about it well because sometimes questions are not asked, and I gave you a clear example of that sometimes it's totally not understandable that a subject is not addressed by the witness, whereas in other circumstance you can say, well, you could have said that you could have left it out, depending on what you were asked. Try to limit yourself to those where I said it bangs into your eyes if it's absent in the comment on a document. If that's the case, make that clear. If it's not the case, perhaps you move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And before you do, if you could just guide me to where you were reading from the document, Mr. Weber. I couldn't find it on the page that was on the screen at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the page before you, it's the second from the bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Where we talk about [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you are commenting upon the 1st Motorised Brigade. Do you consider that the information about them having a shortage of men and rotating shifts to be important or relevant to the assessment or strength of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gathered all possible information about enemy forces, so I included it here because it was not up to me to assess whether something is relevant or not. I put on paper the information that I received and, at a later stage, the analysis department in the corps will find a proper place for this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's again not an answer to the question but let's move on. Mr. Weber, where exactly would you expected the witness to say something about this aspect? Where do I have to look? 1st Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The comments that are on paragraph 14 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 14. One second. Let's see whether something bangs into my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Actually, let me make sure I'm looking at the right statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- 14 is all about positions, not about strength. So, therefore, nothing bangs, at this moment, in my eyes. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just noting because it also discusses deployment. So I will move on. I take your -- the Chamber's note on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is focussing on perhaps deployment and positions but not on strength as a separate issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the document says what it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just one last thing of something that comes up in relation to your associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 1D3076. And if we could have page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 44 of your statement, you claim that Muslims shelled their own hospitals at the time and the document that you referred to is this document. As you can see, the document is highly illegible in parts and where I find this information in the document is on page 3 of the English translation at the top where we see that the person who is explaining this to you heard it from someone else, who is illegible, that Muslims shelled the hospital with five shells. Do you know the name of the person of this report whose name is also illegible or the person that -- who we see to be illegible that this person heard it from?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to go back to the first page to see with whom the interview was made, who provided this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could have the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the first page of the English too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot make it out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually I have no further questions after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Mr. Lukic, any assessment of how much time you would need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can say that after this many documents, I'm not going through every single one, of course, but I will have quite a number of questions. I cannot give the estimate now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this to say that do you think we would finish at the end of today's session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I really doubt that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I would like to encourage you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will encourage myself, too, to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And don't forget, of course, that part of the lengthy time is also because the witness -- and you know the Chamber is not always very much in favour of sweeping statements in many respects needed to be confronted with material which the Defence was aware of, I take it, as well. That causes part of the time consumption. We'll take the break. The witness is invited to follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be -- to enter the courtroom. I nevertheless would like to say a few words about the earlier -- whatever I could call it, a debate, although it's not really a debate, the objection. Mr. Lukic, the question put by Mr. Weber, why didn't you address, the question itself is not objectionable. The question in itself was phrased in such a way that there could be no -- but I understood your observations as an objection to the approach taken by Mr. Weber rather than to the question itself. Now, whether you can object against an approach is a different matter but I said about it what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think that having added now that the question itself was not objectionable, then please keep in mind not to take an approach in which useless questions are asked and take an approach where at least it's always verified by the party itself that the question in that context makes sense to ask the witness. Mr. Lukic, any questions on re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic will now put further questions to you, Mr. Sarenac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good afternoon, Mr. Sarenac.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P6779 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sarenac, you had this discussion not only with the Prosecutor but also with Judge Moloto about what this meant, the accuracy being confirmed, the accuracy of the copy. We see 2nd Lieutenant Zeljko Bambarez typewritten but there is no stamped there. Actually, what kind of procedure is this that you carried out? Is this re-investigation or is this a mere copying of the document?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's mere copying of the document so that it could be used in further procedures in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original statement of Zeljko Bambarez is attached to this. That's what we usually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not conduct interviews or interrogations or not, did you interview Zeljko Bambarez once again?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be seen from this document but as for other moments, other cases, I don't remember. But as soon as this was done, of course an investigation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you referred before your question that this is something the witness discussed with me. What you are asking doesn't arise from what I discussed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you asked him whether he knows about the incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I didn't say so. I asked him about the accuracy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After he had told me that the -- that that sentence he interprets to mean that the document is authentic. That was his own words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's all you were interested about, about the authenticity of the document, then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then the same goes to P6780 and P6781. And I will not have further questions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That gives you more time for more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Hopefully I will finish today then. Then if we can have P6784, please, in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sarenac, this document shows that the command of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade is asking for the involvement of forces and is sending this request to the KP Dom Kula administration, KP Dom Butmir.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the commander inform you about what he had ordered or requested?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not the commander's duty to notify me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. We lawyers sometimes don't know what "of course" means and what "naturally" means because we don't have the professional knowledge in certain fields to know what is to be expected, what is of course, what is a matter of course, et cetera. So did they know -- did he inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any authority over the prisoners in Kula?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in charge of fortification work in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in charge of work like that and I did not carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you approve the use of prisoners from Kula --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm going to stop you here. It seems that the responsibility of this witness for these events becomes the focus where I think it should not be, I put it to the parties. I think that there are two reasons why Mr. Weber raised the issue. First of all, where the witness stated that everyone was provided with the Geneva Conventions, and stopping there, and of course the statements suggest that they were read overnight and that they were obeyed to, that Mr. Weber wanted to test that evidence whether what was suggested by it was the case, not about whether this witness is responsible for that. That's one. Second, I take it that Mr. Weber had, in the back of his mind, that establishing this - and, by the way, we've heard evidence on the matter before the use of prisoners from Kula, from elsewhere, at fortifications - that it doesn't harm the Prosecution's case to -- for the Chamber to hear that again. I think these are the two issues. What now appears is that we are focussing on whether the witness should have known -- he apparently -- he wasn't asked, it's not part of his statement. He was reluctant in the beginning to say that he had any knowledge about it. But the issue is not primarily whether this witness is responsible for all this. I think it's whether it's happened, in what context it happened, whereas the witness here seems to be not the pivotal role in the whole of the hierarchy. And the second, to what extent the statement given by this witness is incomplete to the extent that what is suggested turns out to be not what is presented in the documentation. These are the two issues. And what I know see is we are focussing on whether this witness is responsible, whether he heard it, whether it passed through him, et cetera, which is - it seems to me - not to be the core of the testimony of this witness and of the Prosecution's case in this respect. Mr. Weber, I'm first seeking whether you would basically agree with me. I'm not talking about details but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the two points that you've noted, I believe you're correct. With respect to the fact that challenging the credibility of this witness, we did put to the witness his knowledge and involvement with respect to individuals that were taken from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was that to test the reliability and credibility of this witness, or was it because you wanted to establish that this witness had primary responsibility for it or direct responsibility for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on the position of the witness in the security organ and his awareness of it, we would say that he would have some responsibility if he had awareness to take action about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- it's not your focus, it's just his role in the hierarchy, that's -- which makes him co-responsible for things that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's fair, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let's try to focus on that rather than to hear from the witness again what he feels he's not responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Yes, if you want to comment because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no comments. Only maybe I have to pursue this issue after Mr. Weber's response to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then at least it's clear what the issues are. Let's then stick to those. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I've already asked you this, on behalf of your brigade, did you approve the use of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. That was not within the scope of my work and that was not my obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it that requested the use of prisoners on behalf of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the use of prisoners was usually requested, I mean, by battalion commanders and that went through the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you involved if there would be an incident, if the prisoners would try to escape, if they would be shot at, beaten up, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would never be involved. Only if an incident would occur then we would have to clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As security organ, were you involved in clarifying the situation?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that would happen, because each battalion has its own security organ, then, yes, we would certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us know look at P6785 briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we see before us is an Official Note dated the 10th of April, 1994. This is a report about these four men escaping. Is this one of these incident situations? You've seen this document.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These people that are referred to here, and it is stated that they were working there where you were, were they detained in Kula or where you were?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just read this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not know where the witness is reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you know the answer to the question, tell us. Reading the document, that's what we can do ourselves as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I just wish to -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Answer now.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they finished working, they were taken to the KPD Kula. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. These people who carried out this work within your barracks, were they in danger? Is that the front line, the actual front line? What kind of work did they do? Do you remember today?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll see, this very old man, Vukotic, worked with them and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One - one second. Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just objection, compound question and a couple of them were leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the proper basis for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question -- the first question will be: what exactly was the work that they had done? Where, when, and at what times. Otherwise we are seeking -- we can expect answers like the witness started already with that is since they were working with an old person, it must be, and let's try to avoid that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was more concerned about the time than about the -- my questions. I'll try to do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Sarenac, what kind of jobs did these people do?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vujo Vukotic worked around the barracks such as maintenance, minor repairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. You told us what he did. What did these people do?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were on his team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They prepared the material, they brought it, they had a horse-drawn cart within the compound to transport material.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know - just tell me if you know or not - whether those people were brought there by force or they would, first of all, express their wish to go out and work?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't answer that now. Some jobs needed to be done, and we needed manpower. How they were selected, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said you couldn't answer the question. I have one very simple question: Those four men, where had they been working on that day, if you know. If you don't know, tell us as well. No conclusions, just whether you know or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They worked within the compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Within what compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the compound of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the military detention facility within that compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the military detention facility, a remand prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the document reads that at the end of the working day, the prisoners were taken to a military detention facility for accommodation. This strongly suggests that they were not in that detention facility which you said was the compound but that they were outside. Do you have any comment on that? And could you -- if you have, could you please explain clearly the source of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says below they were not taken to KPD Kula to save fuel; but instead, they were later placed within the barracks called Cica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's no answer to my question but it seems to be an answer to a question you consider to be more important. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know whether they enjoyed some benefits on account of working? Did they get better food? Did they spend more time outdoors?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody received the same food, the troops, us, they, and they enjoyed the same benefits as we all did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, we were looking at a document, that book from Kula that we are not going to call up again because we've already discussed your role and your knowledge thereof. But you were asked whether you had undertaken some steps, and you said you proposed to the commander to replace the military police commander.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you didn't mention any names. A name would help us locate that document, and Judge Orie said it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of that platoon was called Brane; I can't remember his surname now. But unfortunately, a couple of months after this incident, he got killed, but there are records certainly about his deployment and his service because he was dismissed and transferred to another unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what he had done that caused him to be removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He allowed a person who was not authorised to have access to prisoners to apply force to a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can't remember the name, can you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only remember his first name. But I know who I mean and you can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was his full name Brane? Or was it Branko or Branislav?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brane.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if I noted it erroneously, but you seemed to have mentioned one more case when you proposed that a disciplinary procedure be instituted.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the case of Warrant Officer Bugarin, who was a middle-aged man who had been there for quite a while. He was a uniformed serviceman, and he was involved in another case. By negligence of the policemen, he approached prisoners and assaulted them. The commander took disciplinary steps against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Bugarin his name?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Milan Bugarin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was going to mention, Your Honour. And maybe the redaction of the reference on line 17 on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The redaction will be made. Not to be broadcasted. Let's have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document, the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, it is said in the last-but-one paragraph that according to the information available to UNHCR officers, the Muslims in the city have stocks of over 2.500 tonnes of food from humanitarian aid which is not being distributed to citizens. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about abuses of the humanitarian aid arriving into the Muslim-controlled part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that this humanitarian aid is being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't raise UNHCR or humanitarian aid convoys in this witness's information during my cross-examination. I did ask about living conditions inside the city so I kind of was patient with this, but I believe the question now about humanitarian aid could cause quite a new area that I did not explore during cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from being pretty leading, Mr. Lukic, on the matter, the Chamber has received that evidence you are referring to. The witness was asked about whether he received information about the situation in the city. The witness confirmed that and, therefore, whether there may have been stocks elsewhere is something the witness didn't tell us about. You're leading very much in that direction. If the witness has some personal knowledge about it, he may tell us. Do you have any personal knowledge about stocks of humanitarian aid not being used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, therefore, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then look at 6787 recently used by my learned friend, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This morning, the Prosecution showed you this document. At the end of it, your name is typewritten, although there is no signature but we don't object to that. An interview was made with Ferid Jusuf. He explains in the sixth paragraph in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ferid Begic, I take it you are referring to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's B/C/S. It's Ferid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Begic. Jusuf is the name of the father, if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... at least I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... -- I heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... It's Ferid. Ferid is first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ferid; Begic family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph in English, he explains that he received a certificate allowing him to leave Sarajevo, and the military unit that issued the document is cited. On the next page, and it's still the same page in B/C/S, and it says that in Dobrinja, he reported to the police and from there he was directed to the command of the armed forces in the immediate vicinity of the airport. At that command, his certificate was registered, and he was told to cope as best he knows.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you gain any knowledge as to whether civilians were able to leave Sarajevo in the zone under your services, observation?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Civilians did not have a free choice whether to leave Sarajevo or not. They managed in different ways. Sometimes they had to pay a fee in order to leave the city through some secret channels. You couldn't choose your place of residence, whether it would be in Muslim-controlled Sarajevo or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask everybody's leave and assistance if we could only stay five or six minutes longer to finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Weber may have some additional questions as well. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Right now, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Right now you don't. Then I'm looking around, and I don't see anyone jumping up and started crying yet. But I think that Mr. Lukic deserves some compassion and he receives it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I won't go on too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we now look at P6788. The B/C/S version is already on the screen. The English will soon follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's about the interview conducted with Tihomir Vranic. It says a member of Muslim armed forces, a recruit of the 102nd Motorised Brigade. From the name, who would Tihomir Vranic be by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was forcibly mobilised into Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just wait for the question, please. Did you have reports that Muslims forcibly mobilised Serbs who were left behind in the territory they controlled?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They forcibly mobilised all military-age able-bodied Serbs, and they explained it through the official version of the state authorities that everybody was a conscript if they were able-bodied, and our young men hid wherever they could, in basements, behind cupboards, anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly look at P6790.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, Mr. Lukic, for the last issue, it was introduced for purpose of establishing morale, not on how people were recruited to become members of the ABiH forces so -- but let move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the Prosecution also departed from the topics from the documents we introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In re-examination, you are supposed to stay within the limits of the cross-examination. If you want to know what you can raise in cross-examination, you can read Rule 90, what is it, (H), and then you know that you're not limited to what it is. Let's not discuss it. It's a legal issue and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and from your observation, I see that there may be some misunderstanding about --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- this legal matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P6790, please, let's take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a document that says that Natasa Miskin was first in Juka 's unit and then in the HVO and then she defected and came to Serb territory. Miskin, is that a Serb name?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Natasa a Serb name?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that girl very well when she came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that at that time she was about 17 years old. It says here that she and other girls were guarded. Did she tell you whether she had been mobilised? How was it that she came?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've stated that. I wasn't sure that she was mobilised but she made a statement, a statement of her own saying that she had been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It just assists me in following along if Mr. Lukic could tell us where in the document he's referring to the -- to what information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To start with, the age of the informant being 17 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He asked me that during the break. I found the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, searching around, I was able to find that in footnote 1 which actually I believe the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties agree that this is there, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: She would be possibly 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And thank you to my colleague. Could we see 1D03039.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zeljko Vaskovic is the person interviewed here. It says that they had to pay in order to leave. He said to you here, and it's on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was discussed was the morale of soldiers and the Prosecutor asked about that. Now, I would be interested in number one. [In English] I don't know what kind of translation we have here. It doesn't appear it's the same document in English version. To speed up things, I'll just read a portion of paragraph 3 in B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "Nane says that about 70 per cent of the soldiers are in favour of having the war end and in favour of peace as opposed to fanatics, mostly refugees from eastern Bosnia." Did you have any information in your work that Muslim soldiers were also in favour of ending the war and, in your view, according to the information that you gathered, who kept extending that war?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information as follows. The local people of Sarajevo wanted the war to end. However, the people from Sandzak, who had come from the area of Sandzak in Serbia, and who held prominent positions and others who were like them, they did their best to have the war continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was all that I had for you. We stayed a bit longer. Thank you for having answered these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I don't know whether we need the witness to be present for this, for discussing the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will not discuss anything at this moment, anymore, Mr. Lukic, let that be clear. Mr. Weber, any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions from the Bench. This then concludes, Witness, your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may now follow the usher. Mr. Lukic, we'll deal with any administrative matters later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only if it's because of the documents of this witness, I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have -- you asked for five to six minutes. We've used 12 now. That is 100 per cent penalty for those assisting us. We leave it to that for the time being. And I would, nevertheless, use at least two seconds in order to thank all those who have facilitated of course not only Mr. Lukic but also the Chamber to have a briefly extended session. We adjourn for the day. We will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 25th of September, Courtroom I, 9.30 in the morning.
